content: Fundal pressure, also referred to as the Kristeller manoeuvre, involves the application of manual pressure to the upper part of the uterus during the second stage of labor. This pressure is directed towards the birth canal with the aim of facilitating spontaneous vaginal delivery and reducing the duration of the second stage of labor or the need for operative interventions. In some cases, fundal pressure has also been applied using an inflatable belt. Despite its widespread use, the methods of application vary significantly, and there is limited evidence to support its benefits or assess its risks for both the mother and the newborn. This highlights the need for an objective evaluation of its effectiveness and safety. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether fundal pressure is effective in achieving spontaneous vaginal birth, preventing prolonged second stage of labor, or reducing the need for operative delivery. Additionally, the review aimed to explore any adverse effects on maternal and neonatal outcomes associated with the use of fundal pressure. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing fundal pressure (manual or inflatable belt) with no fundal pressure in women with singleton pregnancies in the second stage of labor. Data were collected and analyzed using standardized methods, and the quality of the included studies was assessed. Nine trials were included in the review. Five trials (involving 3057 women) compared manual fundal pressure with no fundal pressure, while four trials (involving 891 women) compared the use of an inflatable belt with no fundal pressure. Blinding of participants and staff was not possible due to the nature of the intervention. Some trials were assessed as having a high risk of bias, and most had design limitations. There was significant heterogeneity in the outcomes reported. For manual fundal pressure compared to no fundal pressure: Manual fundal pressure did not significantly increase the likelihood of spontaneous vaginal birth within a specified time (based on very low-quality evidence). It did not significantly reduce the rates of instrumental births, cesarean births, or operative births (all based on very low-quality evidence). The duration of the second stage of labor was not significantly shortened (based on very low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in neonatal outcomes, such as low arterial cord pH or Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (both based on very low-quality evidence). However, women who received manual fundal pressure were more likely to experience cervical tears compared to those in the control group. No neonatal deaths were reported in the studies that assessed this outcome. Severe maternal morbidity or death was not reported in any of the trials. For fundal pressure using an inflatable belt compared to no fundal pressure: The use of an inflatable belt did not significantly reduce the rates of instrumental births or operative births (both based on very low-quality evidence). In nulliparous women, the inflatable belt was associated with a shorter duration of the second stage of labor (based on very low-quality evidence). However, no data were available for multiparous women. There was no significant difference in the rates of cesarean births, low arterial cord pH, or Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (all based on very low-quality evidence). Third-degree perineal tears were more common in women who received fundal pressure via an inflatable belt. Outcomes such as spontaneous vaginal birth within a specified time, neonatal death, and severe maternal morbidity or death were not reported in any of the trials. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the benefits or harms of fundal pressure, whether applied manually or using an inflatable belt. While the use of an inflatable belt may shorten the second stage of labor in nulliparous women and reduce the rates of operative births, the evidence is limited, and the generalizability of the findings is uncertain. There is also insufficient evidence regarding the safety of fundal pressure for the baby. Furthermore, no evidence exists on the use of fundal pressure in specific clinical scenarios, such as when the mother is unable to bear down due to exhaustion or unconsciousness. Given the widespread use of fundal pressure and its potential application in settings where other methods of assisted delivery are unavailable, further high-quality research is needed. Future studies should include detailed descriptions of how fundal pressure is applied and assess its safety for the baby, perineal outcomes, long-term maternal and infant outcomes, and maternal satisfaction. Research should also evaluate its use in other groups of women, such as multiparous women.
